430.t: Lake camps, picnic bands and bands playing on the gallery
430.s: He remembers lakefront camps with bands every day, his cousin killed by the lake train, bands playing on the gallery before dances, and pianos only in the red-light district.
430.q: Anything else you remember around in there or later on? Later on? Yeah, they had a lot of things happen. Well, you see a millen boy. Gee, that was New Orleans. New Orleans was New Orleans at that time. You see, modern times, I mean, it changed everything. They had a lot of camps. Just like they…

430.s: His father's mother gave basket picnics at Lucien's Pavilion; bands played all the camps on the lake and clubs held Monday picnics.
430.q: Yeah. Oh, I'm one of these have picnics out of lake, a bunch of training up. Mm-hmm. Out there. Mm-hmm. Have a good time all the time. Very good time. You want to smoke a mirror, you know, smoke a mirror. You heard about smoke a mirror. Yeah. You don't know, road smoke. And boy, when you got on…

430.t: White and Black bands side by side at Milneburg
430.s: White and Black camps ran next to each other; ten or fifteen bands played at once, bucking each other, including a Christian band.
430.q: Well yes, I mean, they didn't mix, I mean, you know. But one would run a camp next to the other. Yeah, right, yeah, like that, yeah. Everybody was very friendly and got along very nicely. All musicians, everybody in those days, I mean, that was swell, you know.

903.t: Playing the lakefront camps and floods
903.s: Clayton played weekends at Milneburg camps, walking through backwater when storm tides flooded the boardwalk.
903.q: I used to play out there every Sunday, Saturday. We was playing at the Law Cabin or either at Sam's Camp, and people used to be like that. Sometimes the tires would come in and we had to walk in water about a mile to get to the road. Really? Yeah, the tires would come in backwater, you know. Did…

903.t: Mama Lou's, Happyland and Mary's Camp on the lake
903.s: Clayton recalls leading a band with Andrew Jefferson at Mama Lou's, which closed after she died, plus Happyland and Mary's Camp, and the location of Lincoln Beach.
903.q: She died or so. She was a good woman. She had a gold spot right there. Yeah. They had some other people, in-laws try to take it but they couldn't come up to the seafood, you know, like she did.

188.t: Lake picnic schedules and music over the water
188.s: He describes weekend picnic schedules at Milneburg and West End and how one band's music carried over the water to nearby camps.
188.ch: Own band, lake picnics, day jobs
188.q: you know not one place all a lot of fraternity white picnics all on the lake well we used to have picnic sometime we'll leave home on the Saturday evening it'd get back to Tuesday morning you play a Saturday night dance from April 4th and you get out for a Sunday picnic at Millenburg get to hurry…

188.s: He describes how the camps were built, screened porches, bedrooms, and the lake being filled in during WPA time.
188.ch: Own band, lake picnics, day jobs
188.q: outside yeah and then it's just a porch run all around in the back porch you know they have a restroom and they have a dressing room on each corner for ladies and men you know and then the inside they have bench some of them got benches all the most of the benches outside but they need all that…

138.t: Playing Lake Pontchartrain, Washington Garden and Bucktown
138.s: Laine played Sundays and Wednesdays at Washington Garden, an old hotel at the lake, and describes Bucktown's dancing pavilions and the crowds.
138.q: I played at the Washington Garden at the lake. I played Sunday and Wednesdays at the lake. I played at the Washington Garden at the lake. Washington Garden at the lake on a Wednesday, and Sundays I played private picnics. What was Washington Garden? Was that a campground or something? No, it was an…

138.t: Elmira pleasure ground and photographs of sidemen
138.s: They discuss Sunday picnics at Elmira pleasure ground, then identify Ernie Stevens, Emil Christian, Tony Parenti and others in photos.
138.q: Regular open pavilion, just for the little stuff. Top on it, shed over it, you know. And Mr. Foster had the ballroom right across from the... Mm-hm.

84.t: Sunday all-day picnics at Lake Pontchartrain
84.s: Handy describes the Smokey Mary train, five competing bands on piers, bucking contests and camps with swimming and drinking.
84.q: Honestly, you didn't carry it with four or five coaches on it. I wish you should have needed about seven or eight cause it was packed and jammed all the time. I would get out to the lake around 9, 30, 10 o'clock. And we'd walk about two blocks out on those piers to get to the pier, out on the wharf…

84.t: Weekly dance circuit and a Chicago trip
84.s: Handy lists the week's dances after a lake day, and ends with a brief trip to Chicago with Albert Morgan.
84.q: Yeah, some of them. Some of them. Then some of them used to just jump in there for fun and get drunk like that. Just jump in the water. Close and watch everything. Load it, tennis. Jump overboard. I used to like to play out there. It used to get me to go to Moss Point, Mississippi. Play that…

766.s: Music was all along the lake's camps; Milton worked with Georgie Parker and notes musicians were scarce then.
766.q: He was my Mama Lou's. He was at Mama Lou's. You know, he even passed there. He was my Mama Lou's. He was at Mama Lou's, yeah. When did Lincoln Beach start? He was more close, I mean, in town. Well, I worked at Happa Landon a long time too. I worked with Georgie Park out there a long time.

766.t: Milneburg's decline, amusement park and train
766.s: Milneburg faded around 1929-30; they recall the amusement park, tea garden, train and gravel road.
766.q: That's right. You go walk. Big holes and everything. There was nothing but gravel and old shells. I mean all at Lincoln Beach there was nothing but shells and rocks. I mean it's like you say. I mean you had to have a fold. I mean a real good car couldn't go through there.

174.t: The Japanese Tea Garden at Milneburg and Moreau's camp
174.s: He describes the tea garden's lakeside location, the Smoky Mary train, and playing at Moreau's camp in 1928 with Sidney Miner, his brother and others, often playing late and into breakfast dances.
174.ch: Dance jobs and the opera house
174.q: Well, it was right by the water. The Japanese tea garden set right, no, right at the, right by the lake, you see. And then, well, you had to go on the run, or the walkway to get to the camp. It was not on the camp, it was, you know, right on land, but right at the foot of the lake.

175.t: A.J. Piron's society band; Spanish Fort and West End
175.s: Piron resembled Ben Bernie and played society dates; the pair discuss picnics at Spanish Fort and West End.
175.q: Yeah. Well, I think Ben Burnie, his leg was something he used to wear one of these raised shoes or something like that. Now, whether it was the same leg or not, I don't know. But I always thought any time you saw A.J. Pirone, you saw Ben Burnie. And of course Pirone, he used to have a very…

859.t: Bands and boats on Lake Pontchartrain
859.s: Gabriel recalls the best bands and crowded trains and boats of the lakefront resorts.
859.q: Yeah. Well I liked the Olympia band. I liked the- Was that with Freddie Keppard? That's Freddie Keppard and I liked the Manuel Perez band. All them bands could play, they all was good. The Olympia band, the Superior band, the Imperial band, all those things. We would play out to the lake, I swear.…

247.t: Millenburg camp picnics and lawn parties
247.s: He describes Sunday picnic trains to Milneburg camps, pay of a dollar and a half or so, and lawn parties with gumbo, in the yard or house.
247.q: Tranchino's. Tranchino's. I played that too already, but I know that too. Hey, Ron played that. Huh? Hey, Ron. Peter on Peter, that's right. Oh, God, I only called him this club. What used to happen out at Millenburg? Huh? What used to happen out at Millenburg? I never was there. What used to…

479.t: New Orleans picnics and a mixed black-and-white band at Smith's Cottage
479.s: Picnics were the main work, at West End and Smith's Cottage; he put together a mixed band with Dave Perton and Achille Baquet.
479.ch: Mixed bands and early New Orleans
479.q: Oh, yeah. Most of your work was picnics, wasn't it? In those days, New Orleans used to give a terrible lot of picnics, didn't they? That was all the rage for a time, wasn't it? Out at Nuremberg on a Sunday, if they didn't have 25 or 30 bands, they didn't have two. And out at West End, too? All over…

246.t: Bucking the white bands at the lake camps and the Camellia boat
246.s: Glass recalls bucking with Gallaty, Philly Ray and Sharkey at Milneburg camps, the Camellia boat and excursion train, and how Black and white neighbors once got along.
246.ch: Bands, lake camps and early players
246.q: Yeah. They had Buck Vanville's band there for years. Yeah. The Philly Red. You remember Philly Red? Yeah. You remember Philly Red? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

724.t: Session opening; brother's picnics and the camps where they were held
724.s: Allen opens the tape (Jan 4, 1962). Burbank explains his brother's summer picnics at lakefront camps, the halls, and bands playing on the floor.
724.q: Okay, let me see, I'll check the microphone just to get a little something on here. Today is January the 4th, is that right? Correct. January 4th, 1962, and we're recording at 1515 North Roman Street. Can we get your name on here? Full name? Ah, Boy Bang Senior. And your name? Book Free World. And…

255.s: Asked about Milenburg, he recalls the camps near the lake and the Smokey Mary train.
255.q: Well, they had a few spots where all the roads hadn't built up. You take a Lesion Field hadn't built up. They just only paved a Lesion Field all the way back, said during the... Just a little before the wall. Yep. Just a little before the wall. We had a lot of roads that wasn't built in. But I…

256.s: Weekend camp dances at the lake, where bands competed and he lost his slide.
256.q: Oh, yeah. We used to go out there on weekends, Friday, Saturday, and Sunday. Everybody had a camp, you know. You'd walk out about a block on water. One time I'm playing out there, and I'm full Italian boy. And the water's only up to here, you know, around the camp. So I'm playing, I make a shmear,…

624.t: Playing Milneburg camps and the attic stunt
624.s: Brunies recalls playing at Milneburg with Fisher and Schilling, returning in white suits full of cinders, and slipping up into the attic during dances.
624.ch: Fisher's band and Jack Laine's bands
624.q: Yeah, then I used to go out to Millen Boyd and blow the roofs off the... There's all tin roofs out there. And I'd get up there with fishing and shilling, sometime with Jacqueline. Well, shilling's different, isn't it? Yeah, shilling is still... I talked to him one day. Yeah. And we'd go out there…

431.t: Music and dancing at the lake hotels and Bay St. Louis
431.s: Lake hotels had dance music, and special cruise boats ran to Bay St. Louis.
431.q: that much in those breaks over the water? Yes. There were hotels on the lake. In fact, the man that built the original, Arlie Sater, John Davis, had a hotel on the lake at one time, and they had music in those hotels for dancing, because hardly anything that didn't have dancing that connected with…

710.s: Bailey recalls lawn parties on Taylor Street and Milneburg as a Sunday place for Black people, where Keppard and Petit played.
710.ch: Picnics, lake resorts and lawn parties
710.q: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Well, I used to go to lawn parties up on Taylor Street. I called the lady, called Miss Cole. Yeah, they used to have plenty of lawn parties going on. Every Sunday, they used to have parties. And what I say, they can't have that today on account of the young generation. Too rough.…

265.t: Lake resorts: Milneburg and West End
265.s: He recalls the lakefront resorts, camps with bands, and dancing for forty or fifty cents.
265.q: Well yeah, that's why I mean like the lake, Spanish food, West End, all those places where you could go and that's why most of the people would go. Now, Millenburg was a great big place, you go bathing and it had camps all along. They had a band that played out there, you see, in them different…

571.t: Alice on Spanish Fort, West End and funeral music
571.s: Alice says she never went to picnics or Milneburg, only rode through West End, and heard funeral music at home.
571.ch: Lake boats and brass band practice

21.s: He describes train rides to lakeside pavilions, hours played, clubs that sponsored picnics, basket picnics and the Eastman Farm.
21.ch: Picnics, wagon advertising and saloon work
21.q: Then the, uh, the, uh, what do you call it? The, uh, little pavilion. Yes, little pavilion and the band would play in there. See, they had each side gallery, they danced on the gallery. We played from nine.

45.t: Summer picnics at the lake camps, prices and Lent
45.s: Camps along the lake each had a band for Sunday picnics, paying seven dollars, with cheap whiskey and rent; Lent was slack.
45.q: Oh yeah, on the picnic all night, on our Spanish folk. See, they had camps sitting over the water like you see some of them. They had them all the way out from Little Woods all the way to West End to Bucktown. Good. Them camps sitting on the water.

628.t: Joseph Thomas band and its picnics
628.s: After the two-piece jobs Williams joined Joseph Thomas, whose band played more picnics than any in the city; he describes the trucks, pavilion halls, ticket prices and refreshments.
628.ch: Joseph Thomas band and house parties
628.q: No, it's something in the pavilion. Out on the pavilion they got halls, you know. And down at that time there wasn't no buses, there was trucks. You know, they'd have trucks and clubs and Thomas was working for Solara then. And Solara gave one of the biggest picnics, you know. And then we was…

1008.t: West End, Milneburg and the lakefront bands
1008.s: Morgan describes bandstands, the trolley, the Smokey Mary train, camps over the water and Manual Pavilion.
1008.q: Well, they used to have a bandstand. Mostly they played Dixland music, you know. And they used to have trolley cars ride up. Yeah, I remember that. Yeah. I remember that, yeah. Then they had a little old train down here on the Legendfield Street. We used to call it the Smokey Marys.

279.t: Rappolo at the Valencia and Milneburg picnics
279.s: Hug met Leon Rappolo in 1927 and played at Milneburg picnics.
279.q: I would say my association with Buzzy Williams was really great. And then playing around the spots, being associated with fellows like Chink Morton, old timers like that. They really helped to a great extent. Harry Shields. I met Leon Rapolo one time when I was at the Valencia. And he sat in and…

875.t: Picnics, Milneburg and race at the lakefront camps
875.s: Howard talks about picnics and playing at Milneburg, including a white nightclub, and whether the camps were Black or white.
875.q: I played a lot of picnics this year. We never hear about those usually. In the country? Yeah, in the country. That's where they go.

182.t: Algiers oak-tree picnics and the Big Dorsey story
182.s: He describes Sunday picnics under oak trees with brass bands, and interviewers ask about a Dorsey story from Fess.
182.q: Under the oak trees, yeah. White picnics and colored picnics, they had on the oak trees, big oak trees. They used to have on the Sunday night, Sunday night, you know, they'd have big picnics there. Or they'd have big time there, the brass bands sometimes they played. You see, and I'll open the…

665.t: Lawn parties, picnics and fish fries
665.s: Holiday picnics by clubs at Nine Mile Point and the difference between picnics and fish fries.
665.ch: Penny parties, picnics and fish fries
665.q: oh yeah you used to go uh over the river there at a nine miles point they used to call it on uh picnic uh like monday coming up that's a big picnic thing labor day fourth of july then the different clubs would have their annual picnic just like the two lane the two lane went last saturday on a big…

918.t: Millenburg pavilions, camp picnics, Roppolo's breakdown and the fish fry
918.s: Playing soft at Millenburg pavilions, battle-of-music camp jobs, Roppolo's first signs of illness, a later vacation camp, and the Claiborne Street fish fry.
918.q: end yeah well on the very end was corellas pavilion uh uh uh corellas was in the center excuse me that's where frank christian played with his band frank his brother charlie tax was on drums uh willie guitar on string bass yeah and johnny john reiner on the planet and on the end was a place called…

819.t: Picnics, beer, prices, Spanish Fort and Millenburg
819.s: Picnic pay and prices, Lake Pontchartrain resorts and regret over the lost Millenburg.
819.q: Well you had your fun too. Yeah you had a lot of fun. If you had more fun those days what you're having now. Today it's money

570.s: Penn and Manuel Paul recall many bands playing pavilions at Milneburg and using heavy sticks to be heard.
570.ch: Buddy Petit's death, Milneburg and halls
570.q: That was fun those days when Milenburg was running because you'd go out on a Sunday evening and you'd just know you were going to be around three and four bands out there playing different pavilions. There was a lot of kicks. And that music sounds so good going on the water you know. It sounds…

8.t: Picnic camps and Bechet as a boy listening outside
8.s: Sunday picnic dance halls on the water where several bands played, and young Bechet listening outside, unable to get hired.
8.q: Now, like you take like Spanish folk, Millen Boy, on Sundays, you see. All them little camps out there, they have bands. They give picnics, you know. You got a band, this, you got a band. It'll be five or six bands. And you get in them camps, you know. And we used to go to the windows, stick our…

681.t: Bucktown camps and the lake steamboats
681.s: Bucktown was summer camps with weekend dances; steamers like the Susquehanna and Mandeville ran to Mandeville with mostly black bands, and a wooden leg of Bob Aguilera turned up in the union attic.
681.q: Bucktown was camps. They'd have camps and really, everything happened on like say weekends in the summertime. Where people would go, they'd rent a camp and like instead of going to Florida for a week or two weeks like they do now, they'd rent a camp at Bucktown. You didn't have to travel to go…

635.t: Sunday train excursions, picnics and the one-dollar fare
635.s: Foster describes Sunday excursions by train to country picnics where several bands played and people danced on scraped ground, with baskets of food and Italian claret wine.
635.q: We're just talking to everyone to try to find out how to look. We need information from the musicians who are there, so it's accurate. You see? Like we played, we used to play those excursions every Sunday. They go about 90 miles, 100, I don't know all the things. You mean on the train? We played…

572.s: He describes the open-air Tokyo Gardens at Spanish Fort and Tranchina's restaurant.
572.ch: Wider talk: bands, places and players
572.q: Of course they had, uh, linoleum, uh, that they could roll up and down in case it was raining, and so it wouldn't mess up the dance floor, see, in case it was raining. Mm-hmm. Cause you know out there by the lake, it rains all the time in New Orleans.

290.s: He played once at Lucien's Pavilion near Milneburg, used for banquets.
290.q: Around Millenberg, something like that. Around Millenberg, yeah, around Frenchman, like I said, religion field of Frenchman, around there. Yeah, right in there. Yeah, I played it there one time, I mean. They used to, people used to use it practically every Monday, for some sort of a banquet or…

128.t: New Orleans as one big jazz band: house parties, lawn parties, Milneburg camps
128.s: With no radio or TV, house and lawn parties and lake camps at Milneburg, West End and Bucktown kept bands playing.
128.q: It sounded like the whole town was nothing but one big, constant jazz band. What was it like? Well, in a way, I could say it my way about it. You didn't have no radios. I mean, television and all that. Jukebox and most of them. And any little house party will use. Maybe ordinary people will get a…

292.t: Millenburg, Smokey Mary train, West End and courtship
292.s: Getting to Millenburg and Bucktown by train, Brendan's Pavilion, and going to West End while courting her first husband.
292.q: I didn't go. My sister would go. I didn't know how they went. They went by the old train, Smokey Mary. They used to call the old train out at Millenburg. See that lighthouse at the Spanish Fort? Well, that was formerly Millenburg.

296.t: Fairground picnics and the bands that played them
296.s: Dance music for white or colored fairground and lakefront picnics; Robichaux, brass band and the Eagle band.
296.q: Robichaux and the brass band. And then they had another band.

666.t: West End Roof and arriving by noisy sailboat
666.s: Recollections of the West End Roof, where the interviewer's father played briefly, and Rau's noisy schooner arrivals that stopped the dancing.
666.q: I don't think he played out there very long, no. I remember going out there on two or three occasions and sitting with them. But I never played much at that time. Most of my recollection of the West End Roof was coming in on a sailboat. They would, all the people would watch us coming in there.…

1.t: Lakefront camps and Sunday picnic music
1.s: Camps on stilts at Milenburg, West End and Seabrook hosted Sunday music.
1.ch: Childhood, family and the sounds of New Orleans
1.q: You'd go on the riverfront, where I'm going to take you this week, and you'd see the camps on the riverfront, on the stilts, like you see in an Oriental country. There were camps out there. It was just loaded with camps, and every camp on a Sunday had some kind of a music. And they went out to play…
